Question four. What is a surrogate key, and why prefer it over a natural key? A natural key comes from the source, like customer ID forty-two. A surrogate key is one the warehouse makes up, and it means nothing. That's what lets customer forty-two have two rows: ten oh one while Acme Corp was in the East, ten oh two once it moved West. Each order matches the version it was placed under. Natural keys also change, get reused, or clash when two sources each have a customer forty-two. The natural key stays on the row, so each load can look up which surrogate a new fact gets.

Question five. What are the trade-offs of using a hash surrogate key versus a sequence integer? A hash of the natural key is deterministic. The MD5 of forty-two is the same string in development, in production, and in tomorrow's rebuild, so a fact can compute it without a lookup. Integers are compact: a hundred thousand integer keys built an index under a third the size of the same number of hashes. But an integer has to be handed out once, by one counter, and kept. Number the rows with row number on every rebuild, and a new customer with a lower ID shifts every key after it. On Monday, Acme was key three. On Tuesday, three is Umbrella, and Monday's order reads as theirs. So hashes suit projects that rebuild often, in many environments, and they're common in dbt, the tool these models are usually built with. They can collide, rarely, so test the key for uniqueness either way.
